phases.title: 2 · Starting the Aircraft
phases.lede: Cold and dark to passengers boarding.

frag.v: A sweep of the pedestal, the main panel and the overhead before anything gets power. Everything here should already be in position — you are confirming, not changing.
Batteries alone power only a small part of the aircraft. Everything else needs ground power, the APU, or a running engine.
Not every stand has ground power, and in MSFS smaller airports often do not. That is realistic, not a bug — call a GPU if the airport has one, or run the APU instead.
The FWS starts initialising the moment AC power arrives, from either external power or the APU. Do not run the fire tests until the message has gone and the alarms have played out.

Many airlines now require the packs to be running before passengers board and until deboarding is complete, so the APU goes on even with ground power — the packs need APU bleed air whenever the engines are not running. APU bleed is also required to start the engines.

frag.v: out — on a short flight, before the flight. Descent planning is the pilot's job, not ATC's: they will often give descent instructions, but you must know where your top of descent is and ask for the clearance if it has not come.

What drives the plan: the cruise level, the STAR's altitude constraints, its speed constraints — slowing down while descending is hard — and passenger comfort, since −4000 ft/min is nobody's idea of a good time.

frag.v: Rule of thumb, without the flyPad:
distance = altitude difference × 3 ÷ 1000, plus about 10 % margin
. FL320 down to FL140 is 18 000 ft → 54 NM → about 59 NM. Take less margin into a headwind, more into a tailwind.
Treat the STAR and approach as optional. ATC may vector you to a different runway or shortcut the arrival — but only if you are low enough by then.

If the chart says the transition level is "by ATC" and you are offline, use the real-world D-ATIS, or the transition altitude plus 1000 ft. A SimBrief import fills it in for you.

The A320 draws a downward arrow at its own computed TOD, but the number remains yours to validate.
Managed descent (DES) flies the computed vertical profile and can produce surprisingly high and low vertical speeds. If you are new to it, pull for
instead — it gives the linear descent most people expect.

ATC rarely clears you all the way down in one step, and still expects the STAR's constraints to be met even under a lower clearance. Managed descent handles exactly this: it levels off at the constraint and continues once the constraint no longer applies.

In APPR phase with managed speed, the aircraft targets S speed after FLAPS 1, F speed after FLAPS 2, and V
once the landing flap is selected. Aim to be in CONF 1 at S speed by the time FLAPS 2 is due.

Set FLAPS 2 before the glideslope descent starts — slowing down on the slope is hard, and the flap drag is what keeps you from dropping the gear early just to lose speed. Airbus guidance puts FLAPS 2 at about 2000 ft on the slope, which only works if the speed is already down.
If ATC assigns an approach speed ("160 kt to 5 miles"), pull for selected speed until that point, then push back to managed and take the gear, FLAPS 3 and FLAPS FULL from there.

head: V-Speed
Term
rows: - The highest speed (V) during take-off that you can reject the takeoff and still stop on the runway. — The lowest speed from which a takeoff can be safely continued within the takeoff distance after an engine failure at the critical engine failure speed.
Takeoff safety speed (V) the aircraft attains no later than an altitude of 35 ft (11 m) and is maintained during the 2nd segment of takeoff with one engine failed.
The maximum speed (V) at which a full control deflection in one direction should be made in normal or alternate law.
Speed (V) for flying down the approach.
Maximum structural design limit speed (V) and Mach.
Predictive VFE at next flap/slat position.
Maximum gear Extension speed (V), often lower than the operating speed to prevent gear door damage.
Maximum gear Operating speed (V), which means the max speed for the gear being down.
Airbus for the MAXimum speed (V) for the current configuration, represented by a black and red strip at the top of the airspeed indication.
Minimum speed (V) in the Air that if one engine fails and the other is at TO thrust, you can still control the aircraft with the primary flight controls up to a bank of 5 degrees.
Minimum speed (V) on the Ground that if one engine fails and the other is at TO thrust, you can still control the aircraft with the primary flight controls.
Maximum Operating speed (V), also has MMO for maximum Mach number.
Rotate speed (V). The speed at which the pilot pulls back on the stick to pitch the airplane to the takeoff attitude.
REFerence speed (V) for a normal approach at the 50-foot height.
Stalling speed (V) at which airplane is controllable.
Stalling speed (V) or minimum steady flight speed obtained in a specified configuration.
Stalling speed (V) or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration.
Airbus for when the Stall Warning will activate, represented by a black and red strip at the bottom of the airspeed indicator, when there has been a failure to affect the flight control laws.
Speed (V) for best angle of climb.
Speed (V) for best rate of climb.
Airbus speed (V) for the MAXimum angle of attack (α) that the pilot can achieve in normal law, shown by the top of a red strip at the bottom of the airspeed indicator.

Airbus for the speed (V) that the angle of attack (α) PROTection will become active to stop the aircraft from stalling, shown as being the top of the black and amber strip at the bottom of the airspeed indicator.

head: V-Speed
Term
rows: Minimum speed at which the Flaps may be retracted at takeoff (i.e., CONF 2/3). Also, the minimum speed in approach when in CONF 2 or 3
Minimum speed at which the Slats may be retracted at takeoff. Also, the minimum speed in approach when in CONF 1.
Green Dot speed, engine-out Operating speed with flaps up, best lift-to-drag ratio speed, also corresponds to final takeoff speed.
